title: Arjuna's no to victory
hookLine: Arjuna refuses victory and asks what for; Krishna's answer: act, and offer the fruit.
carry: do the work, offer its fruit to god
tomorrow: sanatana: a name for a religion, or something else here?

cards: A trophy on a shelf, a job offer, a final grade: sometimes the thing worked hardest for gets close, and suddenly it looks strange. Arjuna gets there on a chariot, with the war about to begin. Na.
No. He puts it first, before anything else: na kankshe vijayam krishna. I don't want victory, Krishna.
A warrior says he doesn't want to win.

teach.h: NA KANKSHE VIJAYAM. KIM: WHAT FOR?
teach.b: The whole line: na kankshe vijayam krishna, na cha rajyam sukhani cha. I don't want victory, Krishna, nor a kingdom, nor pleasures. Then a question: kim no rajyena govinda, kim bhogair jivitena va.
Kim: what. What is a kingdom to us, Govinda? What are enjoyments, or life itself?
The prize he came for has become a question. Krishna will answer it, and Hindus have lived by the answer ever since. In chapter two he says: karmany evadhikaras te, ma phaleshu kadachana.

teach.h: YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE ACTION.
teach.b: Your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. Don't let the prize be your reason, and don't cling to doing nothing either.
In chapter nine he goes further: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, do it as an offering to me.
That's why many Hindus close a puja, a meal or a day's work with a few words: Shri Krishnarpanam astu, may this be offered to Krishna. Now the week, inside that answer.
Duryodhana mocked his teacher, and the tradition says acharya devo bhava. Arjuna called Krishna by many names, each a door. The conches sounded, and the shankha still opens worship.
Krishna took the reins. Yudhishthira bowed across the line. Arjuna's bow slipped, and even that was a yoga.
And now kim, what for. The Gita's answer: not for the prize. For the offering.

teach.h: DO THE WORK. OFFER THE FRUIT.
teach.b: So when the grade, the job or the family repair doesn't come out the way you hoped, the work you offered still counts.

how: Many Hindus end a puja, a meal or a task by saying Shri Krishnarpanam astu, may this be offered to Krishna, following the Gita's teaching to act without clinging to the fruit.

games.q: what does “reading the gita's first chapter” mean?
o: the victory songs sung after the battle
Arjuna refuses victory, and Krishna's answer about the fruit of action
Krishna's answer, read before Arjuna's question

games.q: the question and the answer — tap the pairs.
p: may this be offered to Krishna

s: Arjuna refuses because he thinks he'll lose
he says he doesn't want victory, a kingdom or pleasures at all.
Krishna answers: your right is to the action, never its fruits
Gita 2.47: karmany evadhikaras te, ma phaleshu kadachana.
the Gita's answer is to stop acting so nothing can go wrong
Krishna says not to cling to inaction either: do your part, and offer it.

games.q: you finally get the award you chased for months, and it feels strangely empty. what does the Gita's answer to Arjuna's kim suggest?
o: chase a bigger award; the next one will fill the gap.
keep doing the work as an offering, and loosen your grip on the prize.
quit; if the prize is empty, the work was pointless.
games.why: Arjuna asks kim, what for. Krishna answers in 2.47, your right is to the action, never its fruits, and in 9.27, offer it all to me.

practice: Many Hindus close an action with an offering. Bring to mind one thing you're working toward, and let Arjuna's question rest on it for a few breaths: kim, what for.

Then, if you pray, offer it: say softly, Shri Krishnarpanam astu, may this be offered to Krishna, or offer it to God in your own words. If you don't pray, name the work you'll do today, and loosen your grip on how it turns out.

wordCard.voice: Kim: what, and here, what for. Arjuna's question to Krishna, and the Gita's answer: do the work, and let go of the fruit.

orig.note: Sanskrit: kim, what; in Gita 1.32, what for, asked of a kingdom and of life itself.

carryVoice: The line to take with you: do the work, offer its fruit to god. Arjuna asked what for; Krishna answers. A week of verses, closed.
